name: Nettle root

lead: Nettle root is the root of the stinging nettle, with extracts long used in European herbal products for benign prostatic hyperplasia. In supplement circles it is taken to bind SHBG so more testosterone stays free, for better training results and a leaner look.

Lab studies report that components of the root bind SHBG, though Grokipedia says the clinical significance is unclear. A 12-month randomised trial of a root extract in 246 BPH patients reported symptom improvement over placebo; no human trial tests it for testosterone or appearance.

paras: It is taken as a capsule or extract, often in stacks with other testosterone-support supplements. Users generally take it for weeks to months alongside training and judge by bloodwork and gym progress.

Grokipedia, an AI-generated and therefore unverified source, reports rare mild digestive upset, advises against oral use in pregnancy and lists possible interactions with diuretics, blood-pressure and diabetes drugs, lithium and warfarin.

chain: Extract binds SHBG in the lab
angle.text: Nettle root extract is taken to bind SHBG, leaving more free testosterone for muscle and a leaner look. Trials have studied it for prostate symptoms; the testosterone link comes from lab work.

lead: Nettle root refers to extracts of the roots of Urtica dioica, the common stinging nettle. In bodybuilding and testosterone-optimisation circles it is taken as an 'SHBG binder': proponents say that it reduces the amount of testosterone held by sex hormone-binding globulin, leaving more free hormone to support muscle, recovery, skin and the masculine features users are chasing.[1][2][3]

Root extracts also have a long tradition in German phytotherapy for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) [4]. The laboratory basis for the SHBG idea is that a nettle root lignan, (-)3,4-divanillyltetrahydrofuran, binds human SHBG in crystallographic and binding assays [2]. Grokipedia states that the clinical significance of this for testosterone is unclear and unsupported by robust clinical evidence [1].

The human evidence that exists concerns urinary symptoms of BPH, including a 12-month randomised placebo-controlled trial of a root extract in 246 patients [4]. Forum users, mainly on T Nation, discuss nettle root alongside boron and DIM in threads about high SHBG and low free testosterone [3][5].
infobox: Sold as a herbal / dietary supplement

paras: SHBG is a blood protein that binds sex hormones. Proponents say that a nettle root compound occupying SHBG leaves more testosterone unbound. Laboratory studies reported that lignans from the root, including one with high affinity, bind human SHBG, and that aqueous root extracts inhibit SHBG binding to prostate membranes [1]. A 2020 biochemical study examined interactions between SHBG and nonsteroidal ligands that enhance androgen activity [2].

Other laboratory studies examined root extracts on prostate cell lines, reporting an antiproliferative effect on LNCaP cancer cells [6], inhibition of enzyme activity in BPH tissue [7] and inhibition of induced prostate growth in mice [8]. A 2024 study tested a combined saw palmetto and nettle root extract on prostate hyperplasia and inflammation in rats and human cells [9].
No studies found that test nettle root for testosterone, free testosterone or appearance outcomes.

For BPH, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial of 459 mg of dry nettle root extract (Bazoton-uno) enrolled 246 patients for one year; the International Prostate Symptom Score fell from 18.7 to 13.0 on the extract versus 18.5 to 13.8 on placebo (p=0.0233) [4]. Grokipedia also cites a systematic review of randomised trials reporting improved symptom scores with Urtica extracts and no significant adverse effects versus controls, without giving its year [1].

A randomised controlled trial in Pakistan enrolled 60 men with BPH and assessed clinical and biochemical parameters with a nettle root extract [10]. An earlier double-blind multicentre trial in Warsaw compared two doses of a combined nettle root and Pygeum africanum extract in 134 men aged 53 to 84 with BPH symptoms over 8 weeks, reporting significant improvement in urine flow, residual urine and nocturia after 28 days [11]. A comparison of a combined sabal and urtica extract with finasteride in men with BPH analysed prostate volume and outcomes [12]. A 2025 review of nettle roots summarises their constituents and pharmacology [7].

Grokipedia reports that oral use is generally considered safe up to a year at recommended doses with rare mild gastrointestinal effects, that oral preparations are contraindicated in pregnancy, and that possible interactions include diuretics, antidiabetic and blood-pressure drugs, lithium and warfarin [1]. These statements are from an AI-generated source and are not independently verified here.

Stinging nettle has a long record as a food, fibre and folk-medicine plant. Wikipedia notes its appearance in the 10th-century Nine Herbs Charm, Bronze Age nettle textiles found in Denmark, and use of the roots as a yellow dye.[13] Nettle root extracts developed their medical profile in European herbal medicine for prostate complaints, and a 1996 German review listed Urtica dioica root among phytopharmaceuticals used for BPH.[14] Its adoption by strength-sport and men's-health communities as an SHBG-lowering supplement appears in T Nation threads from 2014 onward.[3][5][15]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and physique communities
paras: T Nation posters describe nettle root, boron, magnesium, vitamin D and DIM as options for people whose lab results show high SHBG and low free testosterone.[3][5][16] One user posted a protocol note listing nettle root and boron for high SHBG; another said that boron and nettle root supplements preceded a decline in their SHBG.[17][18] Contributors also note the root and leaf differ, as a reply thread asked whether a store carries root or leaf extract.[19]

lore.intro: Nettle root is discussed in T Nation threads on SHBG and free testosterone, usually as one of several supplements to try, with some users reporting changes in lab values and others cautioning about its effect on DHT.[3][5][17]
